Ignominious

/ig-nuh-MIN-ee-uhs/ - the stress falls on MIN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ignominious means deeply shameful and humiliating.

The mascot's debut was ignominious: he tripped on the flag, slid helmet-first into the tuba section, and was retired by halftime.

Worked Example

The quiz team's captain met an ignominious end to his reign—caught with answer cards taped inside his blazer at the regional final, he was stripped of the trophy on stage while the whole auditorium watched in silence.

Ignominious is heavier than 'embarrassing': it names disgrace that plays out in public and clings to your name afterward—the difference between a stumble and a scandal.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disgraceful: Disgraceful condemns the conduct itself — the act was shameful and wrong, whoever saw it happen. Ignominious shifts the weight onto the aftermath: the public shame that clings to a person afterward. Cheating is disgraceful the moment it happens; being stripped of the trophy on stage is ignominious.

humiliating: Humiliating describes what an experience does to you: it wounds personal pride, and it can do that with no one else watching. Ignominious adds a public stage and a stain that lasts — ignominious defeat makes the papers. You can be humiliated privately; ignominy needs witnesses.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

glorious: bathed in public honor and admiration

honorable: deserving respect for upright conduct

Where it sits · how badly it stains your name — awkward → embarrassing → ignominious

awkward vs. ignominious: Awkward stops far short of ignominious — an awkward stumble is forgotten by morning.

embarrassing vs. ignominious: Embarrassing stops short of ignominious — an embarrassing moment makes you blush, while an ignominious one stains your public name.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ig-

Prefix — ig-: not, without (in- before n)

Root — nomin-

Root — nomin-: name (Latin nomen)

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Ig- (not, without) + nomin- (name) + -ious (full of) = marked by the loss of one's good name. Latin ignominia was the state of having your name — your reputation — publicly stripped away. An ignominious defeat is one that costs the loser exactly that.

Use the root in a new word: nominate

Use the root in a new word: nominate: The council will nominate two volunteers for the service medal on Friday.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Ignominious is for public disgrace with staying power — routs, scandals, downfall. A private fumble is merely 'embarrassing'; save ignominious for shame that makes the papers and follows the name around afterward.
